description:
atlaS NoovA is an independent project led by a Computer Engineering student passionate about software development, technology, and space exploration.

I have experience with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Python, C, C++, and Java. My interests include web development, data science, AI, and building innovative applications.

My goal is to create a meaningful solution using NASA's open data to address a real-world challenge.

details:
WHAT IT DOES

Project atlaS NoovA ("Abandoned but not Forgotten") is an interactive 3D website that tells the stories of the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors rotate a 3D Moon and Mars, click markers placed at each machine's real coordinates, and read what it was, why it was sent, what it discovered and where it is now. It covers 17 artifacts, from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo Lunar Modules to Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10 and 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn and Kepler.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python FastAPI backend serves one JSON file that holds all content, plus the web page. In the browser, Three.js draws the globes, places a marker for each artifact from its latitude and longitude, and flies the camera to the artifact the user selects. A story panel shows a NASA photo, the story, what the machine taught us, and links to NASA sources. A timeline, a "ghost mode" and a "Surprise me" button make exploring playful. A Mission data panel compares how long each machine was designed to work with how long it actually worked, for example Opportunity: 90 days planned, about 14 years achieved.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project is designed for school-age and casual space enthusiasts. It turns silent artifacts into memorable stories, shows how missions often outlast their plans, and sends curious visitors to NASA's own pages to learn more. It is available in English, French and Arabic, with a full right-to-left layout, so more students can enjoy it in their own language.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js, HTML5, CSS3, Google Fonts, VS Code, Git and GitHub. Content and photos come from NASA pages (NASA Science and the NSSDCA catalog).

USE OF AI TOOLS

We used an AI assistant, Claude (by Anthropic), to speed up our work on the code, story text, French and Arabic translations, logo and documentation. The deployment, testing, troubleshooting and final decisions were done by our team.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

We treat each machine as a character, not a data point. Placing every artifact at its real coordinates, showing the "built to last versus actually lasted" comparison, and using ghost mode for the abandoned machines make the stories feel personal. We also created an original logo: a lander under signal arcs, meaning "still transmitting, not forgotten".

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: every story links to a NASA source, and we marked in our documentation which artifacts we verified against NASA pages (6 of 17) and which still need review. Accessibility and reach: three languages, readable fonts, keyboard use, and a fallback so the stories still show if the 3D view cannot load. Simplicity: no database and no login, with all content in one file, so facts are easy to correct and new artifacts easy to add.

LINKS

Live project: https://atla-s-noova.vercel.app/

Code: https://github.com/Mohamed-Amine-Addi/atlaS-Noova
